newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's Bhutto maps drive to recapture power.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's Bhutto maps drive to recapture power.

text.p: Pakistan's ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto prepared on Friday to launch a two-pronged campaign to recapture power, fighting her dismissal in court and taking her case to the streets.
Bhutto said she expected to file a legal challenge next week to President Farooq Leghari's order toppling her government.
She promised to tour the country to whip up support for her Pakistan People's Party (PPP), now that the four-day-old caretaker government had lifted curbs on her movements.
"I am going to fight back," Bhutto told Reuters Television in an interview late on Thursday.
Bhutto was expected to meet advisers on Friday to discuss the court challenge to Leghari's trenchant order, which she called illegal and unconstitutional.
"The lawyers are working on it and I hope (to file the challenge) some time early next week," she said..
Leghari sacked Bhutto on Tuesday with a pre-dawn proclamation that accused her government of rampant corruption and failure to stop rampant extra-judicial killings.
It was the fourth time in 11 years that presidents have used their authority to oust an elected government.
He then had the government in Pakistan's most industrialised province, Sindh, sacked and named an estranged uncle of Bhutto as caretaker chief minister.
Bhutto took solace from the Supreme Court's decision in 1993 to overturn a presidential order sacking former prime minister Nawaz Sharif, leader of the PPP's main rival, the Pakistan Muslim League.
That order contained accusations which were similar to Leghari's.
"I expect the Supreme Court to uphold the decision it gave in 1993 and restore the assembly," Bhutto said.
Bhutto, who was confined to her official residence by security forces for nearly 36 hours this week before being released, said she intended to take her fight to the streets.
"I'll of course need to be touring the country a lot and I'll be doing that," she said, cautioning that there would be "agitation" if elections set for February 3 were not fair.

Bhutto's dismissal poisoned already strained relations with Leghari, who had twice served in her cabinet and been hand-picked by the ousted prime minister. "Ultimately, he (Leghari) took this step because he wanted power," Bhutto said.
"The former comrades-in-arms of the PPP are preparing for a fierce battle against each other," the daily News said.
Bhutto's husband, Asif Ali Zardari, remained in custody in an official resthouse near Islamabad.

Zardari, investment minister in Bhutto's cabinet, was detained without charge on Tuesday in Lahore and transferred to the resthouse, where Bhutto was allowed to visit him in the early hours of Thursday. Bhutto said she was pleased to see he had not been tortured.
Bhutto said she believed that her detained husband would face fabricated charges in connection with the killing of her estranged brother, Murtaza, in September.
"I think they are holding him because they are trying to persuade my sister-in-law (Murtaza's widow Ghinwa) to file a case against him," she declared.
Bhutto said Zardari was being held by the military's Inter-Services Intelligence, but had been placed in police custody on Thursday under an order citing the maintenance of peace.
Zardari is at the centre of corruption allegations swirling around Bhutto's former government, but she said he had done nothing wrong.
